distributed-fallacies.tldr:
• The network is unreliable, slow and changing: all eight fallacies eventually come true.
  • Partial failure is the defining problem: you can't tell slow from dead.
  • Timeouts are guesses, so retried operations must be idempotent.
  • Know the latency ladder: memory ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-region ~100 ms.

distributed-cap.tldr:
• During a partition, choose consistency (CP) or availability (AP); PACELC adds latency vs consistency otherwise.
  • Consistency models range from linearizable to eventual; read-your-writes is often what users need.
  • CAP's C (linearizability) differs from ACID's C (invariants).
  • Pick per data type: balances CP, carts and catalogs AP.
distributed-cap.body:
CAP theorem: during a network Partition, a system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write: linearizability) and Availability (every request to a non-failed node gets a response). Partitions are not optional in real networks, so the real choice is CP or AP when partitioned.

  • CP: refuse or block some requests to stay consistent — ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase, MongoDB (majority writes), banking ledgers.
  • AP: keep answering, possibly with stale data, reconcile later — Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), DNS, shopping carts.

PACELC completes the picture: if Partition, choose A or C; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. DynamoDB/Cassandra are PA/EL; Spanner is PC/EC (pays latency for consistency always).

Consistency models (strongest to weakest)

Model Guarantee Example
Linearizability behaves like a single copy; reads see the latest completed write in real time etcd, Spanner
Sequential all nodes see operations in the same order, not necessarily real-time
Causal causally related operations seen in order by everyone (a reply after its question)
Read-your-writes a client always sees its own writes session stickiness, read from leader after write
Monotonic reads a client never sees older data after newer data
Eventual if writes stop, replicas converge eventually DNS, Cassandra ONE

Stronger models cost coordination (latency, lower availability during partitions); weaker ones push anomaly handling into the application. Most systems mix: linearizable for the money ledger and uniqueness constraints, causal/session guarantees for user-facing reads, eventual for analytics and feeds.

ACID vs BASE: ACID (Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable) for single-node transactions. BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) describes many AP distributed stores.

Interview tip "C" in CAP (linearizability) and "C" in ACID (invariants preserved) are different things. Saying so earns points.

distributed-replication.tldr:
• Single-leader is simplest; replication lag causes stale reads, handled with read-your-writes strategies.
  • Multi-leader and leaderless replication need conflict resolution.
  • Quorums with W + R > N make reads see the latest write.
  • Failover risks lost writes and split brain; use consensus and fencing.
distributed-replication.body:
Replication gives fault tolerance, read scaling and lower latency (geo-replicas).

Single leader (primary–replica): all writes go to the leader; followers apply its log. MySQL, Postgres, Kafka partitions, MongoDB replica sets.

  • Synchronous replication: durable but a slow follower blocks writes. Asynchronous: fast, but leader failure can lose acknowledged writes. Semi-sync: wait for at least one follower.
  • Replication lag causes stale reads: read-after-write anomalies (user updates profile, refreshes, sees the old one). Fixes: read your own writes from the leader for a short window, or track the write's log position and read from a replica that has caught up.
  • Failover risks: lost writes, split brain (two leaders), and choosing timeouts. Solve with consensus-based leader election and fencing.

The read-after-write anomaly

Multi-leader: writes accepted at several leaders (multi-datacenter). Requires conflict resolution: last-write-wins (loses data), merge functions, CRDTs, or application-level resolution.

Leaderless (Dynamo-style): client writes to several replicas and reads from several. With N replicas, writes acknowledged by W nodes and reads querying R nodes, W + R > N guarantees the read set overlaps the latest write.

Text
N = 3, W = 2, R = 2  ->  2 + 2 > 3, reads see at least one up-to-date replica
N = 3, W = 1, R = 1  ->  fast, but reads may be stale (eventual)

Repair mechanisms: read repair (fix stale replicas found during a read), anti-entropy with Merkle trees (background comparison), hinted handoff (a neighbour temporarily stores writes for a down node). Sloppy quorums keep accepting writes during partitions at the cost of guarantees.

distributed-partitioning.tldr:
• Range partitioning enables scans but creates hot spots; hashing spreads load.
  • Consistent hashing moves only ~1/N keys when nodes change; virtual nodes balance load.
  • Hot keys need splitting, caching or salting.
  • Secondary indexes are local (scatter-gather reads) or global (multi-partition writes).
distributed-partitioning.body:
When data or load exceeds one machine, split it into partitions (shards).

Choosing the shard key is the decision you can't easily undo: it should spread load evenly, keep a request's data on one shard (tenant_id, user_id), and match the dominant query. Cross-shard queries become scatter-gather; cross-shard transactions need Sagas or 2PC.

Strategy How Pros Cons
Range key ranges (A–F, G–M…) efficient range scans hot spots (time-based keys)
Hash hash(key) mod N even distribution no range queries; resharding moves almost everything with plain mod
Consistent hashing keys and nodes on a ring adding a node moves ~1/N keys needs virtual nodes for balance
Directory lookup table of key → shard flexible the directory is a dependency

Hot partitions: a celebrity user or a popular product overwhelms one shard. Mitigate by adding a random suffix to hot keys (and fan-in reads), caching, or splitting that partition.

Secondary indexes across partitions: local (each partition indexes its own data, reads scatter-gather to all) or global (index partitioned by the indexed term, writes touch multiple partitions).

Why plain hash mod N is a problem: going from 4 to 5 nodes changes hash % N for ~80% of keys, so almost the whole cache misses or the whole dataset moves. Consistent hashing moves only the keys between the new node and its predecessor (~1/N).

Each key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash. Adding D at position 45 only steals keys in (30, 45] from C. With virtual nodes (each physical node placed 100–256 times on the ring), load spreads evenly and a joining or failing node's share is distributed across many peers instead of one neighbour.

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes

Java
public class ConsistentHashRing<N> {
    private final TreeMap<Long, N> ring = new TreeMap<>();
    private final int virtualNodes;

    public ConsistentHashRing(Collection<N> nodes, int virtualNodes) {
        this.virtualNodes = virtualNodes;
        nodes.forEach(this::add);
    }
    public void add(N node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node);
    }
    public void remove(N node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) ring.remove(hash(node + "#" + i));
    }
    public N nodeFor(String key) {
        if (ring.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("no nodes");
        Map.Entry<Long, N> e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));   // first node clockwise
        return (e != null ? e : ring.firstEntry()).getValue(); // wrap around
    }
    private static long hash(String s) {
        // 64-bit FNV-1a; production code uses MurmurHash3 or xxHash
        long h = 0xcbf29ce484222325L;
        for (byte b : s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) { h ^= b; h *= 0x100000001b3L; }
        return h;
    }
}

Used by Cassandra, DynamoDB, memcached clients, and load balancers needing sticky routing. (Redis Cluster uses a fixed 16384-slot scheme instead; Kafka uses hash mod partition count.)

distributed-consensus.tldr:
• Consensus needs a majority: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures.
  • Raft: randomized election timeouts, terms, log replication committed by majority.
  • Voters only elect candidates whose logs are at least as up to date, preserving committed entries.
  • Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes leases rather than writing your own.
distributed-consensus.body:
Consensus: several nodes agree on a value (or an ordered log) despite failures. It underlies leader election, distributed locks, configuration stores and replicated state machines. Needs a majority (quorum): a cluster of 2f + 1 nodes tolerates f failures (3 nodes → 1, 5 nodes → 2). Even sizes add cost without extra tolerance.

Raft (etcd, Consul, Kafka KRaft, CockroachDB) in brief:

Leader election in a 5-node cluster

Quorum sizes

Cluster size Majority Failures tolerated
3 2 1
4 3 1 (no gain over 3)
5 3 2
7 4 3 (more replication traffic, slower commits)
  1. Roles: follower, candidate, leader. Time is divided into numbered terms.
  2. Leader election: a follower that hears no heartbeat within a randomized election timeout (e.g. 150–300 ms) becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and requests votes. A majority makes it leader. Random timeouts avoid split votes.
  3. Log replication: the leader appends client commands to its log, sends AppendEntries to followers, and marks an entry committed once a majority has stored it; then it applies it to the state machine.
  4. Safety: a node only votes for candidates whose log is at least as up-to-date as its own, so a new leader always has all committed entries. Stale leaders from older terms are rejected.

Paxos solves the same problem (older, harder to understand). ZooKeeper uses ZAB. In application code you rarely implement consensus: you use etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul, or a Kubernetes Lease for leader election.

FLP impossibility: in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash failure, no deterministic algorithm guarantees consensus terminates. Real systems use timeouts (partial synchrony) to make progress.

distributed-time.tldr:
• Wall clocks drift and jump, so they can't order events across machines.
  • Lamport clocks give a causal total order; vector clocks detect concurrent updates.
  • Snowflake and UUIDv7 give sortable ids without coordination.
  • Last-write-wins with timestamps silently drops writes under skew.

distributed-locks.tldr:
• A lock with a TTL can expire while its holder still works (GC pause, network delay).
  • Fencing tokens let the resource reject writes from stale holders.
  • Redis locks are fine for efficiency; correctness-critical locks need consensus plus fencing.
  • Keep critical sections short and operations idempotent.
distributed-locks.body:
A distributed lock ensures only one process does something at a time (run a job, process a resource). Implementations: Redis (SET key value NX PX ttl), ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential nodes, etcd leases, database row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, Postgres advisory locks).

The fundamental problem: a lock with a TTL can expire while the holder is still working (long GC pause, network delay). A second client acquires it, and now two clients act at once, and the first doesn't know.

Lock implementations compared

Redis SET NX PX ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential node etcd lease DB row / advisory lock
Release on holder crash TTL expiry session expiry (heartbeats) lease expiry connection close
Ordering / fairness no yes (watch predecessor node) yes (revision) DB queue
Fencing token build it yourself (INCR) zxid / node sequence revision number version column
Survives failover safely no (async replication) yes (consensus) yes (Raft) yes (if DB is the resource)
Best for efficiency, avoiding duplicate work correctness correctness, Kubernetes-native when the DB is the protected resource

ZooKeeper lock recipe

Watching only the predecessor (not the lock parent) avoids the herd effect where every waiter wakes up on each release.

Fencing tokens fix it: the lock service returns a monotonically increasing token with every grant. The protected resource (DB, storage) rejects writes carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen.

SQL
-- Fencing at the storage layer with a conditional update
UPDATE inventory SET qty = :qty, fence = :token
WHERE sku = :sku AND fence < :token;   -- 0 rows updated = stale holder

Redlock (acquiring a Redis lock on a majority of N independent masters) is debated: it depends on bounded clock drift and pauses. For correctness-critical locks prefer a consensus system (etcd/ZooKeeper) plus fencing; Redis locks are fine for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work) where an occasional double execution is tolerable. See the Redis track for the implementation.

distributed-delivery.tldr:
• At-most-once loses messages, at-least-once duplicates them; exactly-once effects need dedup or transactions.
  • Idempotency keys make retried POSTs safe.
  • 2PC is atomic but blocking; avoid it across microservices.
  • Design operations as "set state" rather than "increment" where possible.
distributed-delivery.body:
Semantics Meaning How
At-most-once may lose, never duplicates send without retry; commit before processing
At-least-once never loses, may duplicate retry until acked; commit after processing
Exactly-once effect happens once at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing, or transactions

True exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is impossible; what systems provide is exactly-once processing (effect): retries plus deduplication or atomic commit of output and progress (Kafka transactions).

Idempotency — applying an operation twice has the same effect as once.

  • Naturally idempotent: PUT /users/1 {…}, DELETE, "set status = PAID", upserts.
  • Not idempotent: POST /payments, "balance += 100", "send email".
  • Make them idempotent with idempotency keys: the client generates a unique key per logical operation; the server stores key → result in the same transaction and returns the stored result on repeat.

Details that matter: scope keys per client/account, store a hash of the request body and reject the same key with a different body (422), return 409 while the first attempt is still IN_PROGRESS, and expire keys after 24–72 hours.

Java
@Transactional
public PaymentResult charge(String idempotencyKey, ChargeRequest req) {
    return idempotencyRepo.findById(idempotencyKey)
        .map(IdempotencyRecord::result)                       // replay: same answer
        .orElseGet(() -> {
            PaymentResult result = gateway.charge(req);
            idempotencyRepo.save(new IdempotencyRecord(idempotencyKey, result)); // PK = key
            return result;
        });
}
// A concurrent duplicate hits the primary-key constraint -> catch and return the stored result.

Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to prepare (vote), then tells them to commit or abort. Atomic, but blocking: if the coordinator dies after prepare, participants hold locks indefinitely. Used inside databases and XA; avoided across microservices (use Sagas).

distributed-ratelimit.tldr:
• Token bucket allows bursts; sliding window counters are accurate and cheap; fixed windows burst at edges.
  • In a cluster keep counters in Redis with atomic Lua; return 429 with Retry-After.
  • Backpressure slows producers; load shedding drops low-priority work early.
  • Propagate deadlines so services don't work on abandoned requests.
distributed-ratelimit.body:
Rate limiting algorithms

Algorithm Idea Pros / cons
Fixed window counter count per minute bucket simple; allows 2× burst at window edges
Sliding window log store each request timestamp exact; memory heavy
Sliding window counter weighted mix of current and previous window accurate enough, cheap
Token bucket tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b; each request takes one allows bursts up to b; most common (AWS, Stripe)
Leaky bucket queue drains at a fixed rate smooth output; adds latency
Java
// Sliding window counter
public class SlidingWindowLimiter {
    private final int limit; private final long windowMs;
    private long windowStart = System.currentTimeMillis();
    private int current, previous;

    public SlidingWindowLimiter(int limit, long windowMs) { this.limit = limit; this.windowMs = windowMs; }

    public synchronized boolean allow() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long elapsed = now - windowStart;
        if (elapsed >= windowMs) {
            previous = elapsed >= 2 * windowMs ? 0 : current;
            current = 0;
            windowStart = now - (elapsed % windowMs);
            elapsed = now - windowStart;
        }
        double weight = 1.0 - (double) elapsed / windowMs;          // overlap with previous window
        if (previous * weight + current < limit) { current++; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}

In a cluster, keep counters in Redis (atomic Lua script) so all instances share them; return HTTP 429 with Retry-After.

Backpressure: let consumers signal producers to slow down (bounded queues, CallerRunsPolicy, Reactive Streams request(n), Kafka's pull model). Load shedding: reject low-priority work early when overloaded so high-priority work stays fast. Timeouts with deadlines: propagate the remaining budget downstream so services don't work on requests the client already abandoned.

Little's law sizes these: concurrency = throughput × latency. At 3,000 req/s and 50 ms per request you need ~150 requests in flight; if latency degrades to 500 ms, the same throughput needs 1,500 — which is why queues and thread pools explode when a dependency slows down.

distributed-patterns.tldr:
• Heartbeats and phi-accrual detectors suspect failures; gossip spreads state in O(log N) rounds.
  • Write-ahead logs give durability; Merkle trees find divergent replicas; Bloom filters skip absent keys.
  • Load balancing: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing, power of two choices.
  • Leases and CDC are building blocks for coordination and data sync.
distributed-patterns.body:
• Heartbeats and failure detection: nodes ping periodically; missing several means suspected dead. Phi-accrual detectors (Cassandra, Akka) output a suspicion level instead of a binary verdict.
  • Gossip protocols: each node periodically exchanges state with a few random peers; information spreads in O(log N) rounds. Membership and failure detection in Cassandra, Consul (SWIM), Redis Cluster.
  • Write-ahead log (WAL): append the change durably before applying it; replay on crash. Postgres, Kafka (the log is the data), Raft.
  • Merkle trees: hash trees to find differing ranges between replicas cheaply.
  • Bloom filters: probabilistic set membership, no false negatives; avoid disk lookups for absent keys (Cassandra SSTables) or block cache penetration.
  • Load balancing algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, consistent hashing (sticky), power of two random choices (pick two at random, use the less loaded — near-optimal and cheap).
  • L4 vs L7 load balancers: L4 routes TCP connections (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 understands HTTP (routing by path/header, TLS termination, retries).
  • Leases: time-bound grants (locks, leadership) that expire automatically if the holder dies.
  • Change Data Capture: stream database changes (Debezium reading the binlog/WAL) into Kafka to sync caches, search indexes and other services.

qa.q: Explain the CAP theorem with an example.
qa.a: When a network partition separates nodes, a system can either reject some requests to stay consistent (CP) or keep serving possibly stale data (AP). Example: a bank balance service picks CP — better to error than show a wrong balance; a product catalog or shopping cart picks AP — better to show slightly stale data than an error. Without partitions you can have both; PACELC adds the latency vs consistency trade-off in normal operation.

qa.q: What is eventual consistency? How do you live with it?
qa.a: If no new writes occur, all replicas converge to the same value eventually. Live with it by designing UIs that show pending states, using read-your-writes where users expect it, idempotent and commutative updates, versioning to detect conflicts, and compensations instead of rollbacks.

qa.q: What is a quorum? Why W + R > N?
qa.a: A minimum number of nodes that must participate for an operation to succeed. With N replicas, if each write is acknowledged by W and each read queries R, then W + R > N means every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so the read includes the latest value.

qa.q: How does consistent hashing work, and why virtual nodes?
qa.a: Nodes and keys are hashed onto a ring; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node only moves keys between it and its neighbour (~1/N of keys) instead of reshuffling all. Virtual nodes place each physical node at many ring points so load spreads evenly and a departing node's keys scatter across many others.

qa.q: How does Raft elect a leader?
qa.a: Followers expect periodic heartbeats. On a randomized election timeout, a follower becomes candidate, increments its term, votes for itself and requests votes. Nodes grant one vote per term, only to candidates with logs at least as up-to-date as theirs. A majority wins; the new leader sends heartbeats. Randomized timeouts make split votes rare.

qa.q: What is split brain and how is it prevented?
qa.a: Two nodes both believe they're leader (e.g., after a partition) and accept conflicting writes. Prevent it with majority quorums (a minority partition can't elect a leader), leases with expiry, and fencing tokens so a deposed leader's writes are rejected.

qa.q: Why can't you rely on timestamps to order events across servers?
qa.a: Clocks drift and NTP corrections can move them backwards, so a later event can get an earlier timestamp and last-write-wins discards the newer write. Use logical clocks (Lamport, vector), a single sequencer (a partition leader), or consensus-assigned ordering.

qa.q: How would you implement a distributed lock safely?
qa.a: Use a coordination service with leases (etcd, ZooKeeper) or Redis SET NX PX with a unique owner token and a Lua compare-and-delete release. Because a holder can pause past expiry, protect the resource itself with fencing tokens. Keep critical sections short and operations idempotent.

Not as pure network delivery: acks can be lost, so senders must retry, so duplicates are possible. Systems achieve exactly-once effects by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing or with atomic commit of results and consumer offsets (Kafka transactions + read_committed).

qa.q: Why avoid two-phase commit in microservices?
qa.a: It's synchronous and blocking: all participants hold locks until the coordinator decides, a coordinator failure can leave them blocked, availability becomes the product of all participants' availability, and many brokers and NoSQL stores don't support XA. Sagas with compensation fit better.

qa.q: Design a rate limiter for an API cluster.
qa.a: Token bucket or sliding window per client key (API key/user/IP), counters in Redis updated atomically via a Lua script (or INCR + EXPIRE for fixed windows), enforced at the gateway. Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers. Consider local pre-limiting to reduce Redis calls, fail-open vs fail-closed if Redis is down, and different tiers per plan.

qa.q: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
qa.a: Vertical: a bigger machine (more CPU/RAM) — simple but capped and a single point of failure. Horizontal: more machines — near-unlimited and fault tolerant but requires stateless services, load balancing, and partitioning/replication for data.

qa.q: How do you generate unique IDs in a distributed system?
qa.a: UUIDs (no coordination; v7 for time-ordering and index-friendliness), Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp + machine id + sequence, 64-bit sortable), database sequences with block allocation (hi/lo), or a central ID service. Watch out for clock rollback with time-based schemes.

A mechanism for a slow consumer to signal a fast producer to slow down, instead of buffering without bound until memory runs out. Examples: bounded blocking queues, TCP flow control, Reactive Streams demand, Kafka consumers pulling at their own pace.

cheat.distributed-cheatsheet:
Why distributed systems are hard

  • The network is unreliable, slow and changing: all eight fallacies eventually come true.
  • Partial failure is the defining problem: you can't tell slow from dead.
  • Timeouts are guesses, so retried operations must be idempotent.
  • Know the latency ladder: memory ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-region ~100 ms.

CAP, PACELC and consistency models

  • During a partition, choose consistency (CP) or availability (AP); PACELC adds latency vs consistency otherwise.
  • Consistency models range from linearizable to eventual; read-your-writes is often what users need.
  • CAP's C (linearizability) differs from ACID's C (invariants).
  • Pick per data type: balances CP, carts and catalogs AP.

Replication: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless, quorums

  • Single-leader is simplest; replication lag causes stale reads, handled with read-your-writes strategies.
  • Multi-leader and leaderless replication need conflict resolution.
  • Quorums with W + R > N make reads see the latest write.
  • Failover risks lost writes and split brain; use consensus and fencing.

Partitioning (sharding) and consistent hashing

  • Range partitioning enables scans but creates hot spots; hashing spreads load.
  • Consistent hashing moves only ~1/N keys when nodes change; virtual nodes balance load.
  • Hot keys need splitting, caching or salting.
  • Secondary indexes are local (scatter-gather reads) or global (multi-partition writes).

Consensus, leader election and Raft

  • Consensus needs a majority: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures.
  • Raft: randomized election timeouts, terms, log replication committed by majority.
  • Voters only elect candidates whose logs are at least as up to date, preserving committed entries.
  • Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes leases rather than writing your own.

Time, clocks and ordering

  • Wall clocks drift and jump, so they can't order events across machines.
  • Lamport clocks give a causal total order; vector clocks detect concurrent updates.
  • Snowflake and UUIDv7 give sortable ids without coordination.
  • Last-write-wins with timestamps silently drops writes under skew.

Distributed locks and fencing tokens

  • A lock with a TTL can expire while its holder still works (GC pause, network delay).
  • Fencing tokens let the resource reject writes from stale holders.
  • Redis locks are fine for efficiency; correctness-critical locks need consensus plus fencing.
  • Keep critical sections short and operations idempotent.

Delivery semantics, idempotency and exactly-once

  • At-most-once loses messages, at-least-once duplicates them; exactly-once effects need dedup or transactions.
  • Idempotency keys make retried POSTs safe.
  • 2PC is atomic but blocking; avoid it across microservices.
  • Design operations as "set state" rather than "increment" where possible.

Rate limiting, backpressure and load shedding

  • Token bucket allows bursts; sliding window counters are accurate and cheap; fixed windows burst at edges.
  • In a cluster keep counters in Redis with atomic Lua; return 429 with Retry-After.
  • Backpressure slows producers; load shedding drops low-priority work early.
  • Propagate deadlines so services don't work on abandoned requests.

Other building blocks: heartbeats, gossip, caching, load balancing

  • Heartbeats and phi-accrual detectors suspect failures; gossip spreads state in O(log N) rounds.
  • Write-ahead logs give durability; Merkle trees find divergent replicas; Bloom filters skip absent keys.
  • Load balancing: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing, power of two choices.
  • Leases and CDC are building blocks for coordination and data sync.
